slides.title: Introduction to Chemistry
bullet_points: Chemistry is the study of matter and its changes.
The word 'chemistry' comes from the ancient Egyptian word 'kēme' meaning 'earth'.
Everything around us is made of chemicals.
Chemistry is essential for meeting our basic needs: food, clothing, shelter, health, energy, clean air, water, and soil.

slides.title: Definition of Chemistry
bullet_points: Chemistry is the science that deals with the:
• Properties of substances
• Composition of substances
• Structure of substances
• Transformations (changes) substances undergo
• Energy released or absorbed during these changes

slides.title: Key Terms in Chemistry
bullet_points: Substance: A particular kind of matter with uniform properties (e.g., gold, silver, water).
Matter: Anything that has mass and occupies space (e.g., book, pencil, air).
Property: An attribute or characteristic of a substance that distinguishes it from others.
Composition: The ingredients or constituents that make up a substance.
Structure: The arrangement and relationships between the parts of a substance.

slides.title: Transformations and Energy
bullet_points: Every substance in our environment is continuously changing.
Changes occur due to both external and internal forces.
Transformation: A marked change in form, nature, or appearance.
These changes are always accompanied by energy changes.
Example: Burning wood transforms it into ash, smoke, and heat energy.

slides.title: Branches of Chemistry: Overview
bullet_points: Chemistry can be divided into five main disciplines:
1. Physical Chemistry
2. Organic Chemistry
3. Inorganic Chemistry
4. Analytical Chemistry
5. Biochemistry

slides.title: Physical Chemistry
bullet_points: Studies macroscopic properties and atomic properties.
Examines phenomena in chemical systems.
Investigates:
• Rates (speed) of chemical reactions
• Energy transfers during reactions
• Physical structure of materials at the molecular level

slides.title: Organic Chemistry
bullet_points: Studies substances containing carbon.
Carbon is one of the most abundant elements on Earth.
Carbon can form over twenty million different chemicals.
Most chemicals in all living organisms are carbon-based.
Examples: DNA, proteins, carbohydrates, fats, plastics, and fuels.

slides.title: Inorganic Chemistry
bullet_points: Studies substances not primarily based on carbon.
Commonly found in rocks and minerals.
Important area: Design and properties of materials for:
• Energy technology
• Information technology
Examples: salts, metals, acids, bases, and metal oxides.

slides.title: Analytical Chemistry
bullet_points: Studies the composition of matter.
Focuses on:
• Separating components
• Identifying components
• Quantifying (measuring) components in samples
Uses complex instruments to analyze unknown materials.
Example: Testing water quality for pollutants.

slides.title: Biochemistry
bullet_points: Studies chemical processes that occur in living things.
Covers basic cellular processes to understanding diseases.
Helps develop better treatments for illnesses.
Examples:
• How enzymes work
• DNA replication
• Photosynthesis
• Metabolism of food

slides.title: Scope of Chemistry
bullet_points: Chemistry affects all aspects of life because all living and non-living things are made of matter.
Chemistry extends to:
• Explaining the natural world
• Preparing people for career opportunities
• Producing informed and patriotic citizens
Key application areas: Agriculture, Medicine, Food production, Building construction

slides.title: Applications of Chemistry
bullet_points: Agriculture: Fertilizers and pesticides
Medicine: Life-saving drugs, vaccines, and treatments
Food production: Preservatives and nutritional enhancement
Building construction: Glass, steel, and cement
Energy: Batteries, fuels, and solar cells
Clothing: Synthetic fibers like polyester and nylon

slides.title: Negative Impacts of Chemistry
bullet_points: Chemistry can also produce dangerous substances.
Toxic chemicals can negatively affect human life and the environment.
Examples of harmful substances:
• Fluorochlorohydrocarbons (CFCs) - damage ozone layer
• Oxides of nitrogen (NOx) - cause acid rain and smog
• Oxides of carbon (CO, CO₂) - contribute to climate change
• Oxides of sulfur (SOx) - cause acid rain

sections.section_title: The Relationship Between Chemistry and Other Natural Sciences

slides.title: Introduction to Science and Chemistry's Role
bullet_points: Science is the process of learning about the natural universe through observation, testing, and generating models.
Science is divided into many branches.
Chemistry is one branch of science.
Chemistry has been called the 'central science'.
Why? It links all other sciences together.

slides.title: Relationship with Biology: Biochemistry
bullet_points: Biology studies living things.
Chemistry and Biology overlap in Biochemistry.
Biochemistry is the study of chemical processes occurring in living matter.
Examples:
• Chemists study compounds from medicinal plants
• Understanding metabolism and digestion
• DNA and protein synthesis

slides.title: Relationship with Geology: Geochemistry
bullet_points: Geology studies rocks and the earth.
Chemistry and Geology overlap in Geochemistry.
Geochemistry studies:
• Processes controlling abundance of chemical compounds in geologic environments
• Composition and distribution of compounds and isotopes
• Formation of minerals and ores

slides.title: Relationship with Physics: Physical Chemistry & Chemical Physics
bullet_points: Physics studies nature and properties of matter and energy.
Chemistry and Physics overlap in two areas:
Physical Chemistry: Applies physics theories to chemical systems
Chemical Physics: Studies chemical processes from a physics perspective
Both deal with:
• Atomic and molecular properties
• Energy and matter interactions

slides.title: Relationship with Medicine: Medicinal Chemistry
bullet_points: Chemistry and Medicine are related in the area of Medicinal Chemistry.
Medicinal chemistry involves:
• Design of pharmaceutical drugs
• Development of drugs
• Synthesis (production) of drugs
Examples: Antibiotics, painkillers, cancer drugs

slides.title: Summary: Chemistry as the Central Science
bullet_points: All fields of science are related and depend on matter.
Chemistry is called the 'central science' because it is the foundation.
Key overlaps:
• Chemistry + Biology = Biochemistry
• Chemistry + Geology = Geochemistry
• Chemistry + Physics = Physical Chemistry & Chemical Physics
• Chemistry + Medicine = Medicinal Chemistry

sections.section_title: The Role Chemistry Plays in Production and in the Society

slides.title: Chemistry in Agriculture: Fertilizers
bullet_points: Chemistry has produced chemical fertilizers.
Types of fertilizers:
• Calcium superphosphate
• Urea
• Ammonium sulphate
• Sodium nitrate
These have greatly increased the yield of fruits, vegetables, and crops.

slides.title: Chemistry in Agriculture: Pesticides
bullet_points: Chemistry has produced pesticides to reduce crop damage.
Types of pesticides:
• Fungicides: Kill fungi
• Herbicides: Kill weeds
• Insecticides: Kill insects
Chemistry also helps produce better-quality plastic pipes for irrigation.

slides.title: Chemistry in Food Production
bullet_points: Chemistry has led to the discovery of different kinds of food preservatives.
Preservatives help store food for longer periods.
Chemistry provides methods to test for adulterants (impurities).
New technologies have improved food's:
• Availability
• Appearance
• Nutritional content
• Flavor
Local example: Preserving raw meat for longer periods.

slides.title: Chemistry in Medicine: Overview
bullet_points: Chemistry has provided many life-saving medicines.
Examples of discoveries:
• Sulfur drugs: Cure for dysentery and pneumonia
• Penicillin: Antibiotic for bacterial infections
• Cisplatin and Taxol: Cancer therapy
• AZT: Fights HIV/AIDS virus multiplication

slides.title: Types of Medical Chemicals
bullet_points: Disinfectants: Kill microbes (e.g., sanitizers, toilet cleaners)
Analgesics: Painkillers (e.g., aspirin, ibuprofen)
Anesthetics: Relieve pain during operations
Antibiotics: Control infection and cure diseases
Antiseptics: Prevent wound contamination by bacteria
Tranquillizers: Reduce tension and mental stress

slides.title: HIV/AIDS Prevention
bullet_points: HIV/AIDS is a pandemic with no curative medication.
Prevention methods (ABC):
• A: Abstain from sexual activity
• B: Be faithful or reduce the number of sex partners
• C: Use a Condom
AZT does not cure HIV/AIDS but fights virus multiplication and prolongs life.

slides.title: Chemistry in Building Construction
bullet_points: Chemistry provides building resources such as:
• Glass
• Steel
• Cement
These help in construction of:
• Safer houses and multi-story structures
• Long-lasting and durable dams and bridges
Example: Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) - largest hydro power project in Africa

slides.title: Summary: Role of Chemistry in Society
bullet_points: Agriculture: Fertilizers, pesticides, and irrigation equipment
Food Production: Preservatives, testing for adulterants, improved quality
Medicine: Life-saving drugs, disinfectants, painkillers, antibiotics
Construction: Materials for safer and durable infrastructure
Chemistry touches almost every aspect of our existence.

slides.title: Introduction to Measurements
bullet_points: Measurement is the comparison of a physical quantity with a fixed standard unit.
Example: On a centimeter scale, the centimeter is the standard.
Measurement is essential in chemistry to:
• Compare properties of substances
• Assess changes from experiments
A measured quantity is always written as a number with an appropriate unit.

slides.title: Common Measuring Devices
bullet_points: Meter stick: Measures length
Burette: Measures volume of liquid dispensed
Pipette: Measures precise volumes of liquid
Graduated cylinder: Measures volume
Volumetric flask: Measures a specific volume
Balance: Measures mass
Thermometer: Measures temperature

slides.title: SI Units (International System of Units)
bullet_points: SI units are the modern metric system.
Adopted in 1960 by the General Conference of Weights and Measures.
There are seven SI base units:
• Length: Meter (m)
• Mass: Kilogram (kg)
• Time: Second (s)
• Electric current: Ampere (A)
• Temperature: Kelvin (K)
• Amount of substance: Mole (mol)
• Luminous intensity: Candela (cd)

slides.title: Temperature Scales
bullet_points: Temperature measures the 'hotness' or 'coldness' of a body.
Heat is a form of energy that flows from hotter to colder bodies.
Three temperature scales: Kelvin (K), Celsius (°C), Fahrenheit (°F)
Relationships:

slides.title: Derived Units
bullet_points: Derived units are obtained by combining base units.
Examples of derived units:
• Area: m² (length × width)
• Volume: m³ (length³)
• Density: kg/m³ (mass/volume)
• Speed: m/s (distance/time)
• Force: Newton (N) = kg·m/s²
• Pressure: Pascal (Pa) = kg/(m·s²)
• Energy: Joule (J) = kg·m²/s²

slides.title: Volume and Density
bullet_points: Volume is the amount of space a substance occupies.
SI unit for volume: cubic meter (m³).
Common laboratory units: liter (L) and milliliter (mL).
1 L = 1 dm³, 1 mL = 1 cm³
Density is mass per unit volume.
Formula: d = m/V
Density is a characteristic property of a substance.

slides.title: SI Prefixes
bullet_points: SI prefixes are used to express larger or smaller quantities.
Common prefixes:
• Tera (T): 10¹²
• Giga (G): 10⁹
• Mega (M): 10⁶
• Kilo (k): 10³
• Hecto (h): 10²
• Deca (da): 10¹
• Deci (d): 10⁻¹
• Centi (c): 10⁻²
• Milli (m): 10⁻³
• Micro (µ): 10⁻⁶
• Nano (n): 10⁻⁹
• Pico (p): 10⁻¹²

slides.title: Uncertainty in Measurements
bullet_points: Every measurement has some degree of uncertainty.
Two types of uncertainty:
1. Systematic Uncertainty: Consistent errors that make values too high or too low (e.g., faulty equipment).
2. Random Uncertainty: Variations without a predictable pattern.
Uncertainty can be expressed as:
• Absolute uncertainty: Value ± uncertainty (e.g., 23.25 ± 0.05 g)
• Percent uncertainty: (absolute uncertainty / measurement) × 100%

slides.title: Precision vs. Accuracy
bullet_points: Precision: Closeness of repeated measurements to each other.
• Good precision = reproducible results.
Accuracy: Closeness of a measurement to the true value.
• Good accuracy = measured value matches the true value.
A measurement can be:
• Precise but not accurate
• Accurate but not precise
• Both precise and accurate
• Neither precise nor accurate

slides.title: Significant Figures (Part 1)
bullet_points: Significant figures are meaningful digits in a measurement.
Rules for identifying significant figures:
1. Non-zero digits are always significant.
2. Zeros between non-zero digits are significant.
3. Leading zeros (to the left of first non-zero digit) are NOT significant.
4. Trailing zeros after the decimal point ARE significant.
5. Trailing zeros in numbers without a decimal point are ambiguous (use scientific notation).

slides.title: Significant Figures (Part 2)
bullet_points: Rules for calculations with significant figures:
Addition/Subtraction: Answer has the same number of decimal places as the least precise measurement.
Multiplication/Division: Answer has the same number of significant figures as the number with the fewest significant figures.
Rounding:
• If first digit to drop is <5, keep the number.
• If first digit to drop is ≥5, round up.
Exact numbers (from counting or definitions) have infinite significant figures.

slides.title: Scientific Notation
bullet_points: Used for very large and very small numbers.
Format: A number between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of 10.
Examples:
Avoids ambiguity in trailing zeros.
Shows correct number of significant figures.

slides.title: Introduction: Chemistry as an Experimental Science
bullet_points: Chemistry is largely an experimental science.
Knowledge comes from laboratory research.
Chemists use computers to study microscopic structure.
Chemists use sophisticated equipment to analyze pollutants.
Many frontiers in biology and medicine are explored at the atomic level.
Chemistry is evidence-based; all statements are based on experiment.

slides.title: The Scientific Method: Overview
bullet_points: The scientific method is a process used to investigate natural phenomena.
It involves creating an objective framework for scientific inquiry.
Four main steps:
1. Observation and Formulation of a Question
2. Data Collection and Hypothesis
3. Testing the Hypothesis (Experiments)
4. Analysis and Conclusion

slides.title: Step 1: Observation and Formulation of a Question
bullet_points: The first step of the scientific method.
Make an observation about a natural phenomenon.
Examples:
• 'Why is the sky blue?'
• 'Why is air invisible?'
• 'What happens when I mix these two chemicals?'
Formulate a clear, answerable question based on the observation.

slides.title: Step 2: Data Collection and Hypothesis
bullet_points: Collect all related data about the observation.
Formulate a hypothesis (a tentative explanation).
The hypothesis could describe:
• The cause of the phenomenon
• The effect of the phenomenon
• The relationship between variables
Example: 'The sky is blue because sunlight is scattered by molecules in the air.'

slides.title: Step 3: Testing the Hypothesis (Experiments)
bullet_points: The hypothesis must be tested scientifically.
Conduct experiments to determine if the hypothesis is supported.
Experiments are designed to:
• Test the hypothesis under controlled conditions
• Gather new data
• Repetition is key to reliable results.
Confidence in the hypothesis increases or decreases based on experimental results.

slides.title: Step 4: Analysis and Conclusion
bullet_points: Analyze the experimental data using mathematical and scientific procedures.
Determine the results of the experiment.
If data supports the hypothesis, it is accepted.
If data does not support the hypothesis:
• It is rejected, or
• It is modified and tested again
After repeated confirmation, a hypothesis can become a 'theory'.

slides.title: Laboratory Safety Rules (Part 1)
bullet_points: 1. Responsible behavior is essential.
2. Wear approved eye protection at all times.
3. Perform no unauthorized experiments.
4. Do not smoke in the laboratory.
5. In case of fire or accident, call the teacher at once.
6. Report all injuries to the instructor immediately.
7. Do not eat or drink anything in the laboratory.

slides.title: Laboratory Safety Rules (Part 2)
bullet_points: 8. Avoid breathing fumes of any kind.
9. Never use mouth suction to fill pipets; use a suction device.
10. Never work alone in the laboratory.
11. Wear shoes in the laboratory (no bare feet or sandals).
12. Confine long hair and loose clothing.
13. Keep your work area neat at all times.
14. Be careful when heating liquids.

slides.title: Laboratory Safety Rules (Part 3)
bullet_points: 15. Always pour acids into water when mixing.
16. Do not force rubber stoppers onto glass tubing.
17. Dispose of excess chemicals properly.
18. Read the experiment before coming to the laboratory.
19. Never point test tubes at anyone.
20. Cover cuts with a bandage or wear gloves.
21. Most important: Think about what you are doing.

slides.title: Common Laboratory Equipment
bullet_points: Safety goggles: Protect eyes.
Latex gloves: Protect hands from corrosive chemicals.
Lab apron/coat: Protect clothing from spills.
Beaker: Mixing, stirring, heating chemicals.
• Has spout for pouring
• Has markings for approximate volume
• Not precise for measuring liquids
Watch glass: Used to cover beakers to prevent contamination.

slides.title: Writing a Laboratory Report
bullet_points: Two types of reports:
Pre-laboratory (Prelab) Report:
• Completed before the experiment
• Ensures familiarity with the procedure
• Answers questions from careful reading of the manual
Laboratory Report:
• Final draft written in ink or typed
• Must be neat with no erasures
• All data must have correct units and significant figures

slides.title: Features of a Good Laboratory Report
bullet_points: Report is written in ink or typed.
No erasures or crossed-out areas.
All data should have correct units.
Significant figures must be correct.
All questions answered with complete sentences.
Sample computations labeled with purpose and correct units.
Multiple pages should be stapled and numbered.
Graphs should have titled axes, labels, and data points.

slides.title: Graphs in Laboratory Reports
bullet_points: Graphs present data in picture form.
Essential features of a good graph:
• Axes must be numbered and labeled.
• Graph must have a title.
• Data points shown as circles, crosses, etc. (not dots).
• Lines should be explained in the title.
• Scales should fill the page.
Example: Plot of density measurements against concentration.

slides.title: Experiment: Measurements and Density
bullet_points: Objective: Learn proper mass and volume measurements.
Determine density of:
• A metal bar
• A salt solution
Evaluate results for precision and accuracy.
Materials: Metal bars, measuring rule, pipets, graduated cylinders, balances.
Safety: Use suction device for pipetting, don't drop metal bars into cylinders.

slides.title: Part I: Mass Measurements
bullet_points: 1. Zero the balance after cleaning the pan.
2. Measure mass of a clean dry 50 mL beaker to nearest ±0.001 g.
3. Record observation in lab notebook.
4. Remove beaker, clean pan, zero balance.
5. Weigh same beaker again and record.
6. Repeat one more time.
7. Calculate average mass of the beaker.
8. Repeat weighing using a second balance (one weighing).
9. Repeat using a third balance (one weighing).

slides.title: Part I: Volume Measurements (Pipet)
bullet_points: Volumetric pipets are designed to 'deliver' (TD) the specified volume.
Never pipet by mouth; always use a suction device.
Rinse pipet with small portions of the liquid to be transferred.
Keep pipet tip under liquid surface while filling.
Release suction device gently and fill pipet to 1-2 cm above calibration line.
Remove suction device and quickly seal the top with your finger.
Adjust meniscus to the calibration mark.
Transfer liquid to the container.

slides.title: Part II: Density of a Metal Bar
bullet_points: Weigh a metal bar on a balance to ±0.001 g. Repeat twice.
Method I (Water Displacement):
• Insert bar into a graduated cylinder with water.
• Record initial and final water levels.
• Calculate volume from difference.
• Repeat twice with different initial water levels.
Method II (Direct Measurement):
• Measure dimensions of the bar with a ruler.
• Calculate volume using V = πr²h (for a cylinder).
• Repeat measurements twice.

slides.title: Part II: Density of a Salt Solution
bullet_points: Method I (Using Pipet):
• Weigh a 125 mL Erlenmeyer flask with stopper.
• Pipet 20.00 or 25.00 mL of salt solution into the flask.
• Reweigh.
• Repeat twice.
Method II (Using Graduated Cylinder):
• Weigh an empty dry 10 mL graduated cylinder.
• Fill with 9-10 mL of salt solution.
• Record volume precisely and reweigh.
• Repeat twice.

slides.title: Evaluating Results: Precision and Accuracy
bullet_points: Relative Average Deviation: Measure of precision.
• Calculated from repeated measurements.
• Lower deviation = better precision.
Relative Error: Measure of accuracy.
• Compare experimental value to accepted (true) value.
• Lower error = better accuracy.
Questions to consider:
• Which method is more accurate? Explain.
• Which method is more precise? Explain.

sections.section_title: Historical Development of the Atomic Theories of Matter

slides.title: Introduction: The Concept of the Atom
bullet_points: The existence of atoms was proposed by early Indian and Greek philosophers around 400 B.C.
They believed atoms were the fundamental building blocks of matter.
Continued subdivisions of matter would ultimately yield atoms.
The word 'atom' comes from the Greek word 'atomos' meaning 'uncuttable' or 'non-divisible'.
Early ideas were mere speculations without experimental evidence.
These ideas remained dormant until revived by John Dalton in the early 19th century.

slides.title: Greek Philosophers: Empedocles
bullet_points: Empedocles (mid-5th century BC) thought all materials are made of four elements:
• Earth
• Air
• Water
• Fire
This idea dominated scientific thought for over 2000 years.

slides.title: Greek Philosophers: Plato and Aristotle
bullet_points: Plato (student of Socrates, teacher of Aristotle) adopted Empedocles' theory.
He coined the term 'element' to describe the four substances.
Aristotle adopted the concept of four elements.
He differentiated elements based on properties:
• Hot vs. Cold
• Wet vs. Dry
Example: Water (cold & wet), Air (hot & wet), Fire (hot & dry), Earth (cold & dry).

slides.title: Democritus and the Atomic Theory
bullet_points: Democritus (460-370 BC) elaborated the atomic theory of matter.
He was a student of Leucippus, who originated the atom concept.
Democritus taught the theory of atomism:
• Atoms are indivisible and indestructible.
• Atoms are the basic components of all matter.
• There are different varieties of atoms with different shapes, sizes, and masses.
This model is called 'the solid sphere' model.

slides.title: The Greek Concept of 'Atomos'
bullet_points: Five major points of the Greek atomic idea:
1. All matter is composed of atoms (too small to see, cannot be split).
2. There is a void (empty space) between atoms.
3. Atoms are completely solid (no void inside).
4. Atoms are homogeneous (no internal structure).
5. Atoms differ in size, shape, and weight.

slides.title: Drawbacks of the Early Greek Philosophers
bullet_points: They tried to understand nature through reason and logic, not experimentation.
They had thought-provoking ideas but didn't justify them with observations.
They dismissed Democritus's theory entirely.
Aristotle and other prominent thinkers strongly opposed the idea of the atom.
Their theory was disregarded and buried until the 16th and 17th centuries.
It took over 2000 years for the atomic theory to be fully appreciated.

slides.title: Scientific Laws vs. Theories
bullet_points: Scientific Laws:
• Generalized observations about relationships in the natural world.
• Based on repeated experiments or observations.
• They describe or predict phenomena.
• They don't explain why the phenomenon exists.
Scientific Theories:
• Explanations of phenomena.
• Based on extensive and repeated experimentation.
• They explain the observations described by laws.

slides.title: Law of Conservation of Mass
bullet_points: Discovered by Antoine Lavoisier in 1789.
Also known as the Law of Indestructibility of Matter.
States that mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.
Total mass of products = Total mass of reactants.
Example: Sugar (3g) + Water (20g) → Sugar Solution (23g)
This law laid the groundwork for modern chemistry.

slides.title: Law of Definite Proportions
bullet_points: Proposed by Joseph Louis Proust in 1799.
Also known as Proust's Law or the Law of Constant Composition.
States that a chemical compound always contains the same elements in the same proportion by mass.
Example: Water (H₂O) always has a mass ratio of 1:8 for hydrogen to oxygen.
Example: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) has a mass ratio of 3:8 for carbon to oxygen.

slides.title: Law of Multiple Proportions
bullet_points: Formulated by John Dalton.
States that when two elements form different compounds, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in a ratio of small whole numbers.
Example: Carbon and Oxygen form CO and CO₂.
In CO: 1.33 g of oxygen combines with 1.00 g of carbon.
In CO₂: 2.66 g of oxygen combines with 1.00 g of carbon.
The ratio is 1:2 (a small whole number ratio).

slides.title: Experiment: Conservation of Mass (AgNO₃ + HCl)
bullet_points: Reaction: HCl(aq) + AgNO₃(aq) → AgCl(s) + HNO₃(l)
Materials: Conical flask, test tube, cotton, thread, balance.
Chemicals: Hydrochloric acid, silver nitrate solution.
Procedure:
1. Place dilute HCl in a conical flask.
2. Put silver nitrate solution in a test tube and suspend it inside the flask.
3. Weigh the flask and contents.
4. Tilt the flask to mix the solutions (white precipitate of AgCl forms).
5. Reweigh the flask and contents.
Observation: Mass before reaction = Mass after reaction.

slides.title: Experiment: Conservation of Mass (Ba(NO₃)₂ + Na₂SO₄)
bullet_points: Reaction: Ba(NO₃)₂(aq) + Na₂SO₄(aq) → BaSO₄(s) + 2NaNO₃(aq)
Procedure:
1. Dissolve 2.61 g of Ba(NO₃)₂ in 100 mL of water.
2. Dissolve 1.42 g of Na₂SO₄ in 100 mL of water.
3. Mix the solutions and stir.
4. Filter off the white precipitate (BaSO₄) and weigh it.
5. Evaporate water from the filtrate and weigh the residue (NaNO₃).
Observation: The total mass of products equals the total mass of reactants.

slides.title: Dalton's Atomic Theory
bullet_points: Proposed by John Dalton in 1803.
First scientific atomic theory based on experimental evidence.
Five postulates:
1. Elements are made of small particles called atoms.
2. Atoms can neither be created nor destroyed.
3. All atoms of the same element are identical (same mass and size).
4. Atoms of different elements have different masses and sizes.
5. Atoms combine in small whole numbers to form compounds.

slides.title: Drawbacks of Dalton's Atomic Theory
bullet_points: 1. Atoms are divisible: Atoms can be subdivided into protons, neutrons, and electrons.
2. Atoms of the same element are not always identical: Isotopes exist.
3. Atoms of different elements can have similar masses: Isobars exist.
4. Atoms do not always combine in simple whole-number ratios: Complex organic compounds (e.g., sugar C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁).

slides.title: Modern Atomic Theory
bullet_points: Modified postulates based on new discoveries:
1. Elements are made of small particles called atoms.
2. Atoms cannot be created or destroyed during ordinary chemical reactions.
3. All atoms of the same element have the same atomic number but may vary in mass number (isotopes).
4. Atoms of different elements are different.
5. Atoms combine in small whole numbers to form compounds.

sections.section_title: Discoveries of Fundamental Subatomic Particles and the Atomic Nucleus

slides.title: Discovery of the Proton
bullet_points: Eugene Goldstein (1886) discovered the proton.
Used a cathode ray tube with a perforated cathode.
Observed 'anode rays' or 'canal rays'.
These rays travel from the anode through the holes in the cathode.
They are positively charged particles.
When hydrogen gas was used, the particles had the highest e/m ratio.
These particles were named 'protons'.

slides.title: Properties of Anode Rays
bullet_points: 1. Travel in straight lines.
2. Consist of material particles.
3. Deflected in electric and magnetic fields (opposite to cathode rays).
4. The nature and e/m ratio depends on the gas in the tube.
5. These particles are simply positively charged gaseous ions.

slides.title: Discovery of the Electron: Cathode Ray Tube
bullet_points: J.J. Thomson (1897) discovered the electron.
Used a Crooke's discharge tube (cathode ray tube).
When high voltage is applied at low pressure, a greenish glow is observed at the anode.
Rays are emitted from the cathode (cathode rays).
Key experiments:

slides.title: Thomson's Experiments on Cathode Rays
bullet_points: Experiment 1: Straight-line travel
• A small object placed between cathode and anode casts a shadow.
• Concludes: Cathode rays travel in straight lines.
Experiment 2: Particle nature
• A light paddle wheel placed in the path rotates.
• Concludes: Cathode rays have mass and kinetic energy (particles).
Experiment 3: Charge
• Cathode rays bend towards the positive plate in an electric field.
• Concludes: Cathode rays are negatively charged.

slides.title: Properties of Cathode Rays
bullet_points: 1. Travel in straight lines.
2. Cause mechanical motion (possess kinetic energy).
3. Properties are independent of electrode and gas used.
4. Have a constant e/m ratio.
5. Are negatively charged.
6. Produce fluorescence on a ZnS screen.
7. Ionise gases.
8. Have good penetrating power.
9. Produce X-rays when they hit metals.

slides.title: J.J. Thomson's Atomic Model
bullet_points: Proposed in 1904.
Known as the 'Plum Pudding' model.
Atoms are positively charged spheres with electrons embedded in them.
Electrons are like 'plums' or 'blueberries' in a 'pudding'.
Local analogy: Watermelon (seeds = electrons, red part = positive matter).
Success: Explained electrical neutrality of atoms.
Failure: Could not explain the stability of atoms or the existence of the nucleus.

slides.title: Millikan's Oil Drop Experiment
bullet_points: Robert Millikan (1909) determined the charge and mass of the electron.
Experiment:
• Sprayed fine oil droplets into a chamber.
• X-rays ionized the air, and electrons attached to oil drops.
• Applied an electric field to balance the gravitational force.
Result:
• Charge of electron = 1.59 × 10⁻¹⁹ C
• Mass of electron = 9 × 10⁻²⁸ g

slides.title: Discovery of the Nucleus: Rutherford's Gold Foil Experiment
bullet_points: Ernest Rutherford (1911) discovered the nucleus.
Experiment: Bombarded a very thin gold foil with alpha (α) particles.
Expected (if Thomson's model correct): α particles should pass straight through.
Observations:
• Most α particles passed straight through.
• Some α particles were deflected at large angles.
• A few α particles bounced straight back.

slides.title: Rutherford's Atomic Model
bullet_points: Conclusion from the gold foil experiment:
• Most of the atom is empty space.
• All positive charge and almost all mass is concentrated in a small central region (the nucleus).
• Electrons orbit around the nucleus.
Planetary Model:
• Similar to planets orbiting the Sun.
• Nucleus is like the Sun, electrons are like the planets.
Diameter of nucleus: 10⁻¹³ cm, Diameter of atom: 10⁻⁸ cm.

slides.title: Drawbacks of Rutherford's Model
bullet_points: 1. Inconsistent with classical electrodynamics:
• A charged particle in circular motion emits energy.
• Electrons would lose energy and spiral into the nucleus, causing the atom to collapse.
2. Could not explain atomic spectra:
• The pattern of lines in the spectrum of atoms.

slides.title: Bohr's Atomic Model
bullet_points: Proposed by Niels Bohr in 1913.
Overcame the limitations of Rutherford's model.
Five principles:
1. Electrons are in specific, circular orbits around the nucleus.
2. Electrons occupy only certain orbits (stationary orbits/shells).
3. These shells are associated with a fixed amount of energy (energy levels).
4. Energy increases with distance from the nucleus (K < L < M < N).
5. Electrons do not lose energy while in a particular orbit.

slides.title: Discovery of the Neutron
bullet_points: James Chadwick (1932) discovered the neutron.
Experiment: Bombarded beryllium with alpha particles.
Observations:
• A paddle wheel rotated (radiation has material particles).
• No deflection in an electric field (particles are neutral).
Conclusion: Neutral particles called 'neutrons' are in the nucleus.
Neutrons explain the discrepancy in atomic masses:
• Carbon has 6 protons but mass is 12 amu (6 protons + 6 neutrons).

slides.title: Summary: Subatomic Particles
bullet_points: Proton: +1 charge, mass 1.0073 amu, found in the nucleus.
Neutron: 0 charge, mass 1.0087 amu, found in the nucleus.
Electron: -1 charge, mass 0.0005486 amu, found outside the nucleus.
Basic atomic model:
• Small, positively charged nucleus (protons and neutrons).
• Electrons revolving around the nucleus in orbits.

sections.section_title: Composition of an Atom and the Isotopes

slides.title: Properties of Subatomic Particles
bullet_points: Electron:
• Charge: -1, Mass: 9 × 10⁻³¹ kg (0.0005486 amu)
• Location: Outside the nucleus
Proton:
• Charge: +1, Mass: 1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ kg (1.0073 amu)
• Location: Inside the nucleus
Neutron:
• Charge: 0, Mass: 1.675 × 10⁻²⁷ kg (1.0087 amu)
• Location: Inside the nucleus

slides.title: Atomic Number and Mass Number
bullet_points: Atomic Number (Z): Number of protons in an atom.
• Determines the identity of the element.
• In a neutral atom, number of protons = number of electrons.
Mass Number (A): Total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.
• A = number of protons + number of neutrons
• Also called the total number of nucleons.
Notation: ˄ᙆX (mass number at upper left, atomic number at lower left).
Example: ¹²₆C (Carbon-12, 6 protons, 6 neutrons).

slides.title: Isotopes
bullet_points: Isotopes: Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
Have the same atomic number but different mass numbers.
Examples:
• Hydrogen: Protium (¹H, 0 neutrons), Deuterium (²H, 1 neutron), Tritium (³H, 2 neutrons).
• Carbon: Carbon-12 (6 neutrons), Carbon-13 (7 neutrons), Carbon-14 (8 neutrons).
Most naturally occurring elements are a mixture of isotopes.

slides.title: Average Atomic Mass
bullet_points: Most elements have isotopes.
Average atomic mass is a weighted average of all naturally occurring isotopes.
Formula: Average Atomic Mass = [(% isotope 1)(mass isotope 1)]/100 + [(% isotope 2)(mass isotope 2)]/100 + ...
Example: Lithium (7 amu, 93% and 6 amu, 7%)
This explains why atomic masses are often not whole numbers.

slides.title: Atomic Mass Unit (amu)
bullet_points: Atomic masses are measured on a scale relative to Carbon-12.
One atom of Carbon-12 is assigned a mass of exactly 12 atomic mass units (amu).
1 amu = 1/12 the mass of a Carbon-12 atom.
The atomic mass unit is also called the Dalton (Da).
Examples:
• Helium-4: 4.0026 amu
• Sulfur-32: 31.972 amu

slides.title: Main Energy Levels (Shells)
bullet_points: Electrons are arranged in energy levels (shells) around the nucleus.
Principle: Electrons fill shells starting from the lowest energy (closest to nucleus).
Shells are designated by:
• Letters: K, L, M, N...
Energy increases with distance from nucleus: K < L < M < N.
Maximum number of electrons in a shell = 2n².
• K (n=1): 2 electrons
• L (n=2): 8 electrons
• M (n=3): 18 electrons
• N (n=4): 32 electrons

slides.title: Electronic Configuration
bullet_points: Electronic configuration is the arrangement of electrons in shells.
Rules:
• Fill electrons starting from K shell.
• Valence shell (outermost) can hold a maximum of 8 electrons.
Example: Sodium (11 electrons): 2, 8, 1
Example: Calcium (20 electrons): 2, 8, 8, 2
Atomic diagrams can be drawn to show this arrangement.
Electron configuration determines the chemical properties of an element.

slides.title: Valence Electrons
bullet_points: Valence electrons: Electrons in the outermost shell of an atom.
They are the most easily lost, gained, or shared in chemical reactions.
They determine the element's chemical properties and reactivity.
Example: Silicon (2, 8, 4) has 4 valence electrons.
Example: Argon (2, 8, 8) has 8 valence electrons.
Elements with 8 valence electrons (noble gases) are stable and unreactive.

sections.section_title: Historical Development of Periodic Classification of the Elements

slides.title: Introduction: Why Classify Elements?
bullet_points: As more elements were discovered, scientists needed a system to organize them.
Accurate measurements of atomic masses were available.
Scientists observed that chemical behavior might be related to atomic mass.
Early attempts at classification included Dobereiner's Triads and Newland's Law of Octaves.

slides.title: Dobereiner's Triads (1829)
bullet_points: Johann Dobereiner identified groups of three elements (triads) with similar properties.
The atomic weight of the middle element was the arithmetic mean of the other two.
Examples:
Only a few such triads existed, so it couldn't be generalized.

slides.title: Newland's Law of Octaves (1864)
bullet_points: John Alexander Newlands arranged elements in increasing order of atomic weight.
He observed that the properties of every eighth element are similar to the first.
Like the first octave in music: Do, Re, Mi, Fa, So, La, Si, Do.
Examples: Li, Be, B, C, N, O, F, Na (Na similar to Li).
Limitations:
• Inert gases were not yet discovered.
• The pattern failed after calcium.

slides.title: Mendeleev's Periodic Law
bullet_points: Dmitri Mendeleev (Russia) and Lothar Meyer (Germany) independently proposed the Periodic Law.
Mendeleev's Periodic Law:
• The physical and chemical properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic weights.
Mendeleev's Periodic Table (1871):
• 63 known elements arranged in periods (horizontal) and groups (vertical).
• Left gaps for undiscovered elements.
• Predicted their properties with remarkable accuracy.

slides.title: Features of Mendeleev's Periodic Table
bullet_points: Periods (horizontal rows):
• 7 periods (series).
• 1st, 2nd, and 3rd: Short periods.
• 4th, 5th, 6th, and 7th: Long periods.
Groups (vertical columns):
• 8 groups (I to VIII).
• Subgroups A and B.
• Group IA: Alkali metals.
• Group IIA: Alkaline earth metals.
• Group VIIA: Halogens.
• Group O (later added): Noble gases.

slides.title: Merits and Demerits of Mendeleev's Table
bullet_points: Merits:
• Systematic study of elements.
• Predicted the existence and properties of undiscovered elements.
• Led to the discovery of new elements.
Demerits:
• Some elements were placed incorrectly (e.g., Ar (40) before K (39)).
• Co (58.9) before Ni (58.6).
• Did not explain why properties repeat.

slides.title: Modern Periodic Law
bullet_points: Proposed by Henry Moseley (1913).
Modern Periodic Law:
• The physical and chemical properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers.
This solved the problems of Mendeleev's table.
The modern periodic table is based on atomic number.

slides.title: Structure of the Modern Periodic Table
bullet_points: Periods (horizontal rows): 7 periods.
• Period 1: 2 elements (H, He)
• Periods 2 & 3: 8 elements each.
• Periods 4 & 5: 18 elements each.
• Period 6: 32 elements.
• Period 7: 32 elements (many radioactive/synthetic).
Groups (vertical columns): 18 groups.
• Main groups (A groups): 1A to 8A.
• Subgroups (B groups): 1B to 8B.

slides.title: Relationship: Electron Configuration and Position
bullet_points: Elements in the same period have the same number of electron shells.
Example: Na (2,8,1) is in period 3.
Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons.
Example: F (2,7) and Cl (2,8,7) are both in Group VIIA.
The group number for main group elements equals the number of valence electrons.
Example: Sodium (1 valence electron) is in Group IA.

slides.title: Block Classification of Elements
bullet_points: s-block: Last electron enters an s-orbital.
• ns¹ (alkali metals), ns² (alkaline earth metals).
p-block: Last electron enters a p-orbital.
• ns² np¹⁻⁶ (Groups IIIA to VIIIA).
d-block: Last electron enters a d-orbital.
• (n-1)d¹⁻¹⁰ ns⁰⁻² (transition metals).
f-block: Last electron enters an f-orbital.
• (n-2)f¹⁻¹⁴ (n-1)d⁰⁻¹ ns² (lanthanides and actinides).

sections.section_title: The Major Trends in the Periodic Table

slides.title: Atomic Radius (Atomic Size)
bullet_points: Atomic radius: One-half the distance between the nuclei of two adjacent atoms.
Trends:
• Across a period (left to right): Atomic radius decreases.
• Reason: Increasing nuclear charge pulls electrons closer.
• Down a group (top to bottom): Atomic radius increases.
• Reason: Addition of electron shells.
Example: Li > Be > B > C > N > O > F (decreasing size).

slides.title: Ionization Energy
bullet_points: Ionization energy: The minimum energy required to remove an electron from a gaseous atom in its ground state.
Trends:
• Across a period: Increases (more difficult to remove electron).
• Reason: Increasing nuclear charge, smaller radius.
• Down a group: Decreases (easier to remove electron).
• Reason: More shielding, larger radius.
Example: Li < Be < B < C < N < O < F (increasing IE).

slides.title: Electron Affinity
bullet_points: Electron affinity: The energy change when an electron is added to a gaseous atom to form a negative ion.
First electron affinity is usually negative (exothermic, energy released).
Trends:
• Across a period: More negative (stronger tendency to gain electron).
• Down a group: Less negative (weaker tendency to gain electron).
Nonmetals have higher electron affinities than metals.
Halogens have the highest electron affinities.

slides.title: Electronegativity
bullet_points: Electronegativity: The tendency of an atom in a molecule to attract shared electrons towards itself.
Developed by Linus Pauling.
It is a dimensionless property.
Trends:
• Across a period: Increases.
• Reason: Increasing nuclear charge.
• Down a group: Decreases.
• Reason: More shielding.
Fluorine is the most electronegative element (4.0).
Cesium is the least electronegative element (0.7).

slides.title: Introduction to Chemical Bonding
bullet_points: Most elements do not exist in their atomic form.
Atoms combine to form molecules or compounds.
Atoms are held together by attractive forces called chemical bonds.
A chemical bond is the force that holds atoms together.
Atoms form bonds to become more stable.

slides.title: The Octet Rule
bullet_points: Proposed by Gilbert Lewis.
Octet Rule: Atoms tend to form compounds in ways that give them eight valence electrons.
Eight valence electrons = stable noble gas configuration.
Exceptions: Hydrogen and Helium need only 2 electrons (duet rule).
Ways to satisfy the octet rule:
1. Losing valence electrons (metals).
2. Gaining valence electrons (nonmetals).
3. Sharing valence electrons (nonmetals).

slides.title: Ions: Definition and Formation
bullet_points: Ion: An atom or molecule with a net electrical charge.
Cation: A positively charged ion (atom loses electrons).
• Example: Na⁺, Ca²⁺, Al³⁺
Anion: A negatively charged ion (atom gains electrons).
• Example: Cl⁻, O²⁻, NO₃⁻
Ionization: The process of a neutral atom losing or gaining electrons.

slides.title: Ionic Bond Formation
bullet_points: Ionic bond: The electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
Usually formed between a metal and a nonmetal.
Metals lose electrons to form cations.
Nonmetals gain electrons to form anions.
Example: Sodium chloride (NaCl):
Na⁺ + Cl⁻ → NaCl (ionic compound)

slides.title: Lewis Dot Formulas for Ionic Compounds
bullet_points: Lewis symbol: The chemical symbol of the element with valence electrons shown as dots.
Shows the transfer of electrons in ionic bond formation.
Example: Sodium chloride (NaCl)
• Na· → Na⁺ + e⁻
Example: Magnesium oxide (MgO)
• ·Mg· → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻

slides.title: Properties of Ionic Compounds
bullet_points: 1. Form crystals (crystalline solids).
2. High melting and boiling points.
3. Hard and brittle.
4. Soluble in polar solvents (like water).
5. Conduct electricity when dissolved in water or in molten state.
6. Have high density.

slides.title: Explanation of Ionic Compound Properties
bullet_points: Crystals: Regular 3D structure of alternating ions.
High melting points: Strong electrostatic forces between ions require a lot of energy to break.
Brittle: Shifting ions brings like charges together, causing repulsion and fracture.
Soluble in water: Water molecules are polar and can separate ions.
Conduct electricity: Ions are free to move in solution or molten state.
High density: Ions are closely packed.

slides.title: Covalent Bond Formation
bullet_points: Covalent bond: A bond formed when two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.
Occurs between nonmetals.
Electrons shared are called bonding electrons.
Types of covalent bonds:
• Single bond: One pair of electrons shared (H₂, Cl₂).
• Double bond: Two pairs shared (O₂, CO₂).
• Triple bond: Three pairs shared (N₂, C₂H₂).

slides.title: Covalent Bond Formation: Examples
bullet_points: Single bond: H₂
• H· + ·H → H:H or H-H
Single bond: Cl₂
• :Cl· + ·Cl: → :Cl:Cl: or Cl-Cl
Double bond: O₂
• :O· + ·O: → :O::O: or O=O
Triple bond: N₂

slides.title: Polarity in Covalent Bonds
bullet_points: Nonpolar covalent bond: Equal sharing of electrons.
• Occurs between identical atoms (H₂, Cl₂).
• Electronegativity difference is 0 or very small.
Polar covalent bond: Unequal sharing of electrons.
• Occurs between different atoms (HCl, H₂O).
• Electronegativity difference is between 0.5 and 2.0.
• Partial charges develop: δ⁺ (less electronegative), δ⁻ (more electronegative).

slides.title: Polar and Nonpolar Molecules
bullet_points: Nonpolar molecule:
• No net dipole moment.
• Can be nonpolar bonds or polar bonds arranged symmetrically.
• Examples: H₂, CO₂, CCl₄, CH₄.
Polar molecule:
• Net dipole moment.
• Contains polar bonds arranged asymmetrically.
• Examples: H₂O, NH₃, HCl.
Water (H₂O) is polar: bent shape, net dipole.
Carbon dioxide (CO₂) is nonpolar: linear shape, dipoles cancel.

slides.title: Coordinate Covalent Bond (Dative Bond)
bullet_points: Coordinate covalent bond: A covalent bond where the shared electron pair is provided by only one of the bonded atoms.
Conditions:
• One atom has a lone pair of electrons.
• The other atom has an empty orbital.
Examples:
• Formation of ammonium ion (NH₄⁺): NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺
• Formation of hydronium ion (H₃O⁺): H₂O + H⁺ → H₃O⁺
• Formation of Al₂Cl₆.

slides.title: Properties of Covalent Compounds
bullet_points: 1. Usually gases or liquids at room temperature (some soft solids).
2. Low melting and boiling points (except diamond).
3. Poor conductors of electricity (except graphite, HCl solution).
4. Soluble in nonpolar solvents, insoluble in water.
5. Reactions are slower than ionic compounds.
6. Have low density.

slides.title: Explanation of Covalent Compound Properties
bullet_points: Gases/liquids: Weak intermolecular forces between molecules.
Low melting/boiling points: Weak intermolecular forces require little energy to overcome.
Poor conductors: No free electrons or ions (except exceptions).
Soluble in nonpolar solvents: 'Like dissolves like' principle.
Slow reactions: Bond breaking requires high energy.
Low density: Molecules are loosely packed.

slides.title: Metallic Bond Formation
bullet_points: Metallic bond: The force of attraction between metal cations and a sea of delocalized electrons.
Occurs in metals.
Sea of Electrons Model:
• Metal atoms release their valence electrons.
• These electrons form a mobile 'sea' of electrons.
• The metal cations are immersed in this sea.
• The attraction between cations and electrons holds the metal together.

slides.title: Properties of Metals
bullet_points: 1. Good conductors of electricity and heat.
• Free-moving electrons carry charge and thermal energy.
2. Malleable: Can be hammered into thin sheets.
• Ions can slide past each other without breaking the bond.
3. Ductile: Can be drawn into wires.
4. Luster: Shiny appearance.
• Electrons reflect light.
5. High melting and boiling points.

slides.title: Factors Affecting Metallic Bond Strength
bullet_points: 1. Number of valence electrons: More electrons = stronger bond.
• Magnesium (2 valence electrons) has stronger metallic bond than sodium (1 valence electron).
2. Charge on the metal ion: Higher charge = stronger bond.
• Al³⁺ has stronger bond than Na⁺.
3. Size of the metal ion: Smaller ion = stronger bond.
• Li⁺ has stronger bond than Cs⁺.
Transition metals have very strong metallic bonds because they can involve more d-electrons.

slides.title: Summary: Types of Chemical Bonds
bullet_points: Ionic Bond:
• Metal + Nonmetal
• Transfer of electrons
• Strong electrostatic attraction
• Crystalline, high melting point, conducts when dissolved/molten
Covalent Bond:
• Nonmetal + Nonmetal
• Sharing of electrons
• Forms molecules
• Low melting point, poor conductor
Metallic Bond:
• Metal + Metal
• Sea of delocalized electrons
• Conducts electricity and heat, malleable, ductile
